pos: n. (Ulfilas, c. 311–383, bishop among the Goths and translator of the Scriptures into Gothic, an Arian in his doctrine of the Son)
etymology: Gothic Wulfila, little wolf, a diminutive; Latinized Ulfilas and also written Ulphilas.
biblical_def: Ulfilas was consecrated bishop about AD 341 and sent to the Goths beyond the Danube, among whom he laboured some forty years. He did what no man had yet done for a barbarian people: he made an alphabet for a tongue that had none, and with it put the Scriptures into Gothic. Fragments survive, chief among them the Codex Argenteus, and they are the oldest substantial monument of any Germanic language. In this he stands in the line of Act 2:8, where men heard the wonderful works of God “every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born,” and of Rom 10:14, which asks “how shall they hear without a preacher?” The vernacular Scripture is not a Reformation invention; it is the apostolic instinct, and Ulfilas obeyed it a thousand years before Wycliffe. But the gospel he carried was not the gospel. Ulfilas held the Homoian Arianism of the court bishops who ordained him: the Son is like the Father, but not of one substance with Him. He therefore gave the Goths a Bible in their own speech and a creed that denied the Godhead of its subject, and through him Arianism became the religion of the Gothic nations for two centuries. The translation was a gift; the doctrine was a wound.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to translate, in its literary sense, as to interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
webster_full: TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
2. To explain. [See Interpret.]
3. To transfer; to convey from one place to another.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people.
corruption_summary: Modern accounts praise Ulfilas as the apostle of the Goths and pass over in a clause the fact that what he planted was Arianism.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard treatment makes Ulfilas a hero of translation and a footnote of heresy. That inverts the weight. A Bible in the vernacular is a means; the doctrine preached from it is the end. Ulfilas gave the Goths the text of Joh 1:1 — “and the Word was God” — while teaching them that the Word is a creature, however exalted. The result was not a half-gospel but a different one, and when Alaric and Theodoric ruled in Italy and Spain they ruled as Arians because Ulfilas had catechized their fathers. Translation without orthodoxy multiplies error in the mother tongue.

The recovery is to hold both together as the Reformers did. Tyndale laboured for the plough-boy and for the Nicene faith at once; the vernacular Scripture and the confession of one substance with the Father are not rivals. What is honourable in Ulfilas is honourable: he loved a despised people enough to make them letters. What is condemnable is condemnable: he denied the eternal deity of the Son, and no philological achievement covers it. The church owes him thanks for the alphabet and owes Athanasius thanks for the faith.
roots_summary: Greek glossa (G1100), tongue, language; hermeneuo (G2059), to interpret; logos (G3056), word.
roots_lines: Greek glossa (G1100) — tongue, hence a language; Acts 2:8, 1 Corinthians 14:19.
Greek hermeneuo (G2059) — to interpret, to translate; John 1:42, Hebrews 7:2.
Greek logos (G3056) — word, the Son in His eternal being; John 1:1.
Greek akouo (G191) — to hear; Romans 10:14.
Hebrew goyim (H1471) — the nations, the Gentiles; Psalm 117:1.
usage: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the warrant for his labour.
“every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8) — the vernacular principle, kept.
“and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — the clause his creed denied.

pos: n. (Arnobius of Sicca, d. c. 330, African rhetorician converted late in life, author of the seven books Against the Nations)
etymology: Latin Arnobius, a North African name; he is called Arnobius the Elder to distinguish him from the fifth-century Arnobius the Younger.
biblical_def: Arnobius taught rhetoric at Sicca in Numidia and was, by his own account, a scorner of Christ until late in life. Converted under Diocletian, he offered his bishop the seven books Against the Nations as the proof of his sincerity. The work is a sustained assault on the absurdity and immorality of the pagan gods, and in that it does the work of Act 17:23, declaring the God whom the heathen “ignorantly worship,” and of Rom 1:23, which names the exchange of “the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man.” He is a witness that the apologetic duty of 1Pe 3:15 — “be ready always to give an answer” — was felt in the African church under persecution. But Arnobius is also a warning. He was a new convert with a rhetorician's training and almost no knowledge of the Scriptures, and it shows. He argues that the soul is not naturally immortal but is a middle thing, perishable unless God grant it life; he is vague on creation, uncertain about the Old Testament, and content to attack paganism without stating the gospel. His zeal outran his instruction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apology as a defence; something said or written in defence or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.
webster_full: APOL'OGY, n. An excuse; something said or written in defence or extenuation of what appears to others wrong, or unjustifiable.
2. In Theology, a defence of the Christian religion against its opposers.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
Rom 1:23
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
corruption_summary: Arnobius shows that an apologist may demolish the opponent and still not preach Christ, and that zeal is no substitute for catechism.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern apologetic industry repeats Arnobius's error at scale. It is possible to win the argument against unbelief — to show the folly of idols as he did, that “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4) — and never once to set out sin, substitution and the resurrection. Arnobius had the rhetoric and lacked the doctrine; much that passes for apologetics now has the arguments and lacks the gospel. A defence that leaves a man persuaded paganism is silly but ignorant of Christ has not obeyed 1Pe 3:15, for the hope to be accounted for is a definite hope.

The second corruption is the modern willingness to let his doctrine of the soul pass as an interesting early option. It is not an option. Arnobius taught a conditional immortality in which the soul perishes unless God sustains it, and that error is the root from which annihilationism grows. Scripture gives immortality to God alone in His own right — “Who only hath immortality” (1Ti 6:16) — but it nowhere teaches that the wicked cease to be. The recovery is to receive a man's labour where it is sound and to put a new convert under instruction before he is put in print.
roots_summary: Greek apologia (G627), a verbal defence; eidolon (G1497), an image, an idol; agnoeo (G50), to be ignorant.
roots_lines: Greek apologia (G627) — a reasoned defence; 1 Peter 3:15, Philippians 1:17.
Greek eidolon (G1497) — an image, an idol; 1 Corinthians 8:4.
Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant of; Acts 17:23.
Greek aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible; Romans 1:23.
Hebrew atsab (H6091) — an idol, a thing shaped; Psalm 115:4.
usage: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15) — the duty he undertook.
“Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you” (Act 17:23) — the pattern he half kept.
“Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4) — the burden of his seven books.

pos: n. (Eunomius of Cyzicus, d. c. 393, leader of the extreme Arian party, who taught that the Son is unlike the Father and that the divine essence is comprehensible to man)
etymology: Greek Eunomios, from eu, well, and nomos, law — well-ordered; a name his doctrine did not deserve.
biblical_def: Eunomius was the ablest and boldest of the later Arians. Where Arius had said the Son was unlike the Father in substance and left it there, Eunomius built a system. He taught that the one name proper to God is agennesia, unbegottenness, and that this name expresses the divine essence itself; therefore whatever is begotten is of another essence, and the Son is anomoios, unlike, the Father. From this he drew the conclusion that stung the orthodox most: that man may know the essence of God as God knows it, for the essence is given in a name the mind can grasp. Basil of Caesarea answered him in five books and Gregory of Nyssa in twelve. Their reply rests on Deu 29:29, that “the secret things belong unto the LORD our God,” and on Rom 11:33, “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out.” God is known truly in what He reveals and never exhaustively in His essence. Against the Christology the answer is Joh 10:30, “I and my Father are one.” Eunomius died in exile, his party extinguished within a generation, but his two errors — a reduced Son and a comprehended God — have never stopped returning together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incomprehensible as not to be comprehended or understood; beyond the reach of human intellect; inconceivable.
webster_full: INCOMPREHEN'SIBLE, a. That cannot be comprehended or understood; beyond the reach of human intellect; inconceivable.
2. Not to be contained; that cannot be included within limits.
God is incomprehensible, and his ways past finding out.
scriptures: I and my Father are one.
The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen.
corruption_summary: Eunomius is the pattern of the rationalist who shrinks the Son in order to enlarge his own mind, and both halves of that trade are still offered.
corruption_paragraphs: The Eunomian claim that the divine essence is comprehensible is the native instinct of every theology that will not bow. It survives wherever God is defined as whatever the reasoner can fit in his categories, and it survives in the popular form that says any doctrine beyond the mind's compass — Trinity, two natures, eternal decree — may be set aside for that reason. Scripture forbids the move: the revealed things belong to us and to our children, the secret things belong to the LORD, and “whom no man hath seen, nor can see” (1Ti 6:16) is said of the God who has nevertheless made Himself truly known in His Son.

The second corruption is the modern habit of treating the fourth-century controversy as a power struggle over words rather than a contest for the gospel. It was not a quarrel about a syllable. If the Son is unlike the Father in substance, then the One who died is a creature, the atonement is the death of a creature, and no creature can bear the wrath of God for the elect. Nicaea was not a committee's preference; it was the church confessing that the Redeemer is God of God. The recovery is Basil's and Gregory's: distinguish the knowledge God gives from the essence God keeps, and hold the Son to be of one substance with the Father.
roots_summary: Greek anexereunetos (G419), unsearchable; agennetos, unbegotten (the Eunomian watchword); heis (G1520), one.
roots_lines: Greek anexereunetos (G419) — unsearchable, not to be traced out; Romans 11:33.
Greek heis (G1520) — one, used of the Father and the Son in John 10:30.
Greek aphtharsia and athanasia (G110) — immortality, proper to God alone; 1 Timothy 6:16.
Hebrew sathar (H5641) — to hide; the secret things of Deuteronomy 29:29.
Greek homoousios — of one substance, the Nicene term Eunomius denied.
usage: “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30) — the word his system could not carry.
“The secret things belong unto the LORD our God” (Deu 29:29) — against a comprehended essence.
“how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out” (Rom 11:33) — Gregory's answer in a line.

pos: n. (Aetius of Antioch, d. c. 367, deacon and dialectician, founder of the extreme Arian party called Anomoean, nicknamed the Atheist)
etymology: Greek Aetios, from aetos, an eagle. His opponents called him ho atheos, the godless, for the consequence of his doctrine.
biblical_def: Aetius rose from a goldsmith's bench to be the sharpest logician of the Arian cause, and he is the teacher behind Eunomius. He was ordained deacon at Antioch and set himself to prove by syllogism that the Son is anomoios — unlike the Father — publishing three hundred short propositions to that end. His method was pure Aristotelian dialectic applied to the being of God: define the Father as the Unbegotten, observe that the Son is begotten, and conclude a difference of essence. The orthodox did not answer him chiefly by better logic but by Scripture and by naming the method itself as the error. Col 2:8 stands over his whole career: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men.” So does 1Ti 6:20, with its warning against “oppositions of science falsely so called.” Aetius was deposed, exiled under Constantius, briefly restored under Julian the Apostate, and died without a church. He is remembered because he shows what the Arian premise becomes when a fearless man follows it all the way down: not a lower Christ, but no Christ at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dialectic as logic; that branch of logic which teaches the rules and modes of reasoning.
webster_full: DIALEC'TIC, n. Logic; that branch of logic which teaches the rules and modes of reasoning.
DIALEC'TIC, a. Logical; argumental.
2. Pertaining to the art of reasoning.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
corruption_summary: Aetius is the standing proof that a method may be rigorous and its conclusion blasphemous, and that reason set over revelation does not stay neutral.
corruption_paragraphs: The error in Aetius is not that he reasoned but that he made reason the judge of what God has said. Given his definitions his syllogisms were tight; the definitions were the heresy. This is the permanent temptation of the theological academy, and it is why Pro 3:5 says “lean not unto thine own understanding” in the same breath as it commands trust with the whole heart. Scripture does not forbid logic; it forbids logic enthroned. The same move is made today whenever a doctrine plainly taught is rejected because it will not reduce to a syllogism the reasoner already accepts.

The second corruption is the respectability his kind of rigour still buys. Aetius was admired for his acuteness while he was emptying the Godhead, and the church has repeatedly mistaken sharpness for soundness. 1Co 1:20 asks “where is the disputer of this world?” and answers that God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. The recovery is to test the conclusion by the Word and not the Word by the conclusion, and to hold that the Son is of one substance with the Father because Scripture reveals it, whatever a man's definitions require.
roots_summary: Greek philosophia (G5385), love of wisdom; suzetetes (G4804), a disputer; gnosis (G1108), knowledge.
roots_lines: Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy, used in warning; Colossians 2:8.
Greek suzetetes (G4804) — a disputer, a debater; 1 Corinthians 1:20.
Greek gnosis (G1108) — knowledge, the science falsely so called; 1 Timothy 6:20.
Greek kenophonia (G2757) — vain babbling, empty sound; 1 Timothy 6:20.
Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, not to be leaned upon; Proverbs 3:5.
usage: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8) — the verse his career illustrates.
“where is the disputer of this world?” (1Co 1:20) — the question put to his acuteness.
“oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20) — his three hundred propositions named.

pos: n. (Socrates Scholasticus, c. 380–after 439, lawyer of Constantinople and church historian, author of an Ecclesiastical History continuing Eusebius from 305 to 439)
etymology: Greek Sokrates; the epithet scholastikos means an advocate or lawyer, and distinguishes him from the Athenian philosopher.
biblical_def: Socrates Scholasticus was a lawyer, not a cleric, and his seven books take up the story where Eusebius laid it down. He is the most useful of the Greek church historians because he is the most careful: he quotes documents at length, names his sources, corrects himself in a second edition when better evidence reached him, and tells of the faults of bishops he admires. He writes in the spirit of Luk 1:3, having “perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order,” and his labour serves the end of Psa 102:18, that “this shall be written for the generation to come.” Nearly all that is known of the Novatianists comes through him, and he is the chief witness for the reign of Theodosius II and the troubles at Alexandria. He is not a theologian and does not pretend to be; he judges controversies more by their fruit in peace or tumult than by their doctrine, which is his great limitation. But the church owes much of its memory of the fourth and fifth centuries to a layman who thought the record worth keeping straight, and Deu 32:7 commands exactly that remembering.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of events in the order in which they happened, with their causes and effects.
webster_full: HIST'ORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states; a narration of events in the order in which they happened, with their causes and effects.
2. Narration; verbal relation of facts or events; story.
3. Knowledge of facts and events.
scriptures: Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Deu 32:7
Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
corruption_summary: A historian who weighs doctrine by the quiet it produces will always prefer the compromise to the confession, and that is Socrates's blind spot and ours.
corruption_paragraphs: Socrates's instinct is irenic: he deplores contention and tends to find the fault in whoever disturbed the peace. Applied to the Arian crisis that instinct is disastrous, for the peace of the church was bought at Nicaea by a word some thought needlessly divisive. The same habit governs most church history written now, which treats doctrinal firmness as a sociological problem and ecumenical calm as the obvious good. 1Co 10:11 says the record is “written for our admonition,” and admonition requires that the historian say who was right.

The second corruption is the use made of his candour. Because Socrates reports the sins of orthodox bishops, he is quarried by modern writers to show that the Nicene party was no better than its opponents and that the outcome was therefore political. That is a misuse of an honest man. His willingness to record a failure is evidence of his truthfulness, not of the equivalence of the parties. The recovery is to take the documents he preserved as a gift and to judge the controversies by the Scriptures he did not much consult.
roots_summary: Greek kathexes (G2517), in order, in succession; grapho (G1125), to write; Hebrew zakar (H2142), to remember.
roots_lines: Greek kathexes (G2517) — in order, successively; Luke 1:3, Acts 11:4.
Greek grapho (G1125) — to write; Psalm 102:18 in the Septuagint sense, 1 Corinthians 10:11.
Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition, instruction by warning; 1 Corinthians 10:11.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to keep in mind; Deuteronomy 32:7.
Hebrew dor (H1755) — a generation; Psalm 102:18.
usage: “to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3) — the historian's commission at its best.
“This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — why the record is kept.
“Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations” (Deu 32:7) — the duty he served.

pos: n. (Salamanes Hermias Sozomen, c. 400–c. 450, lawyer of Constantinople and church historian, whose nine books cover the years 324 to 425)
etymology: Greek Sozomenos, from sozo, to save — being saved. Often cited as Sozomenus.
biblical_def: Sozomen was born in Palestine of a family converted from paganism, trained in law, and settled at Constantinople, where he wrote the Ecclesiastical History he dedicated to Theodosius II. He leaned heavily on Socrates Scholasticus and did not conceal it, but he added much of his own: the monks of Egypt and Syria, the conversion of the nations beyond the empire, the affairs of Palestine he knew at first hand. His purpose is doxological, not merely annalistic. He writes to shew “to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done” (Psa 78:4), and he stands in the line of Luk 1:1, where many “have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration” of what is believed. Where Socrates is the better lawyer, Sozomen is the better churchman and the worse critic: he is credulous about wonders, fond of the ascetics, and quick to see a judgment of God in a reverse of fortune. Yet his conviction that the history of the church is the record of God's acts is nearer the truth than the modern annalist's studied neutrality, and Mal 3:16 promises that such a book of remembrance is kept in heaven as well.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicle as a historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
webster_full: CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
2. In general, a history.
CHRON'ICLE, v.t. To record in history or chronicle; to record; to register.
scriptures: Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Luk 1:1
Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us,
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.

And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
corruption_summary: Sozomen's fault is credulity about wonders, and his virtue — that history is God's doing — is the thing modern history has lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Sozomen receives the miraculous on slender evidence, and the monastic marvels he repeats helped build the medieval traffic in relics and saintly prodigies. A Reformed reader honours his reverence and refuses his method: the wonders attested in Scripture are attested by God; the wonders attested by a pious rumour are not. The discipline is to test every claim, for the same Word that records the raising of Lazarus commands that spirits be tried.

The opposite and now far commoner corruption is the writing of church history as though God were not in it. Sozomen believed that Dan 2:21 was true of the empire he lived in, that God “removeth kings, and setteth up kings,” and so he looked for the hand of providence in the fall of a usurper. The modern academic treatment excludes that explanation in principle and then reports a church driven by politics, ambition and economics alone — an account that is not more objective, only differently committed. The recovery is Sozomen's premise with the critic's care: the works are God's, and they must still be proved.
roots_summary: Greek diegesis (G1335), a declaration, a narrative; Hebrew caphar (H5608), to recount; zikkaron (H2146), a memorial.
roots_lines: Greek diegesis (G1335) — a narrative, an orderly declaration; Luke 1:1.
Hebrew caphar (H5608) — to recount, to tell; Psalm 78:4.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial, a remembrance; Malachi 3:16.
Greek biblion (G975) — a book, a scroll; Revelation 20:12.
Hebrew tehillah (H8416) — praise; Psalm 78:4.
usage: “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4) — his stated purpose.
“many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration” (Luk 1:1) — the company he joined.
“a book of remembrance was written before him” (Mal 3:16) — the record above his own.

pos: n. (Sulpicius Severus, c. 363–c. 425, Aquitanian lawyer turned ascetic, author of the Chronicle and of the Life of Martin that founded Western hagiography)
etymology: Latin Sulpicius, a Roman gentile name, with the cognomen Severus, grave or austere.
biblical_def: Sulpicius Severus was a wealthy advocate of Aquitaine who, after the death of his wife, gave up the courts for an ascetic life on his own estate. Two works came of it. The Chronicle is a sober history of the world from the creation to his own day and is the best early account of the Priscillianist affair, which he condemned the bishops for settling by the sword. The Life of Martin is another matter. Written while Martin of Tours was still living, it crowds his career with prodigies — demons expelled, the dead raised, a pine felled by a word — and it became the model every later saint's life imitated. Sulpicius thought he was honouring a faithful bishop. What he in fact supplied was the literary machinery of the cult of the saints: a holy man whose relics heal, whose intercession is sought, and whose power is told in the very terms Scripture reserves for Christ and His apostles. Act 10:26 is the apostolic reflex he lost sight of — Peter raising Cornelius with “Stand up; I myself also am a man” — and 1Ti 2:5 is the doctrine his book quietly crowded out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hagiography, in its root sense, as the writings of the holy men; and a legend as a chronicle of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins.
webster_full: LEG'END, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins and at the refectory of religious houses.
2. An idle or ridiculous story told respecting saints.
3. Any memorial or inscription.
scriptures: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man.

And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
corruption_summary: Sulpicius wrote to honour a good bishop and handed the medieval church the template for venerating him, which is how the cult of the saints began in good intentions.
corruption_paragraphs: The Life of Martin is the headwater of a great corruption. Within a century the pattern was fixed: the saint works wonders in life, his tomb works them after death, and the faithful address him for help. Scripture leaves no room for it. There is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5), and the angel in Rev 19:10 refuses the worship offered him with “See thou do it not…worship God.” Rome formalized what Sulpicius popularized, and the Reformation's recovery of the one Mediator was in large part a dismantling of the shrine-piety his book made imaginable.

The right use of a faithful predecessor is given in Heb 13:7: “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow.” Follow the faith, not the relic. Sulpicius deserves honour for condemning the execution of the Priscillianists, a stand few churchmen of his age would take, and for a Chronicle that is honest where his Life is credulous. But his legacy is the standing warning that devotion to a man, however holy, becomes within a generation a rival to Christ, and that the church must honour its dead the way Hebrews does — by imitating their faith and preaching their Lord.
roots_summary: Greek mesites (G3316), a mediator; proskuneo (G4352), to worship, to do obeisance; mimeomai (G3401), to imitate.
roots_lines: Greek mesites (G3316) — a mediator, a go-between; 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 9:15.
Greek proskuneo (G4352) — to worship, to prostrate; Revelation 19:10.
Greek mimeomai (G3401) — to imitate, to follow; Hebrews 13:7 in sense.
Greek anthropos (G444) — a man, Peter's own word of himself; Acts 10:26.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, to rule; Hebrews 13:7.
usage: “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5) — the doctrine his book obscured.
“Stand up; I myself also am a man” (Act 10:26) — the apostolic refusal of veneration.
“whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) — the lawful honour of the dead.

pos: n. (Salvian of Marseilles, c. 400–c. 480, presbyter and moralist, author of On the Government of God, who read the fall of Roman Gaul as God's judgment on a nominally Christian people)
etymology: Latin Salvianus, from salvus, safe, whole; the same root as salus, salvation.
biblical_def: Salvian watched the Vandals and Goths overrun the richest provinces of the West and wrote the one book of the age that refused to blame the barbarians. In On the Government of God he argues that Rome fell because Rome deserved to fall: that a people baptized and catechized had become more rapacious, more lustful and more cruel than the heathen at its gates, and that God governs the world in righteousness and had therefore given the empire over. His companion work, Against Avarice, turns the same knife on the church's own greed. The texts are his: “judgment must begin at the house of God” (1Pe 4:17), and Amos's terrible logic, “You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amo 3:2). He will not let his countrymen shelter in their baptism, any more than Jeremiah would let Judah shelter in the temple: “Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD” (Jer 7:4). Salvian is uneven as a historian and given to rhetorical excess, but no writer of the fifth century saw more clearly that privilege increases guilt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines judgment, in theology, as the right or power of judging; and the final judgment as the last sentence passed on mankind.
webster_full: JUDG'MENT, n. The act of judging; the act or process of the mind in comparing its ideas, to find their agreement or disagreement.
4. The right or power of passing judgment; as, let us leave this to the judgment of the court.
7. In Scripture, the spirit of wisdom and prudence; also, a calamity, a punishment inflicted by God.
scriptures: For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?
Amo 3:2
You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
Jer 7:4
Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these.
Rom 2:24
For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you, as it is written.
corruption_summary: Salvian's thesis — that God judges a nominally Christian nation more severely than a pagan one — is the hardest word a comfortable church can hear, and the first one it explains away.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader meets Salvian with two ready evasions. The first is to call his reading of events a pre-scientific confusion of history with providence, as though the fall of a civilization could not be God's act. The second is to grant that God judges, and to assume He judges the other party. Salvian forecloses both. He addresses the baptized and the respectable, and his charge is that the very people who held the name blasphemed it, so that “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you” (Rom 2:24). The nation that names Christ and lives in avarice stands nearer judgment than the nation that never heard, and the church is the first address of the sentence.

The recovery Salvian presses is self-examination rather than cultural lament, and it cuts against the use his book now gets. He is sometimes enlisted to prove that empires collapse from moral decay, a thesis any moralist can hold without the gospel, and the point is lost. His argument is not that virtue preserves nations but that God governs them righteously and begins His reckoning at His own house. The answer is not a better civilization but repentance, beginning with the ministers of the church he indicted for their greed.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, of covenant knowing; Amos 3:2.
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie, lying words; Jeremiah 7:4.

“therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amo 3:2) — privilege as aggravation.

pos: n. (Paulus Orosius, c. 375–after 418, Spanish presbyter, pupil of Augustine, author of the Seven Books of History Against the Pagans)
etymology: Latin Orosius, of uncertain derivation; his first name Paulus is attested only later.
biblical_def: Orosius fled the barbarian invasion of Spain, reached Augustine at Hippo about 414, and became his pupil and errand-man. Augustine sent him to Palestine to carry the case against Pelagius to Jerome, and on his return set him to write the historical companion to the City of God: a universal history proving that the calamities of the pagan past were as great as those the pagans blamed on Christ. The Seven Books were the result, and for a thousand years they were the West's textbook of ancient history, read beside Scripture in every monastery. Orosius's governing conviction is Dan 2:21, that God “changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings,” and Act 17:26, that He “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation.” Empires rise and fall at His word, not Fortune's. As history his work is careless, polemical and sometimes plainly wrong; he bends a date to make a point and counts a plague as an argument. As theology of history it is sound where it matters: Psa 75:7, “God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines providence, in theology, as the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
webster_full: PROV'IDENCE, n. The act of providing or preparing for future use or application.
2. Foresight; timely care; particularly, active foresight, or foresight accompanied with the procurement of what is necessary for future use.
3. In theology, the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.
scriptures: Dan 2:21
And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Psa 75:7
But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
corruption_summary: Orosius proves that a true doctrine of providence does not excuse false history, and that apologetic urgency is the commonest reason for handling evidence badly.
corruption_paragraphs: Orosius wrote to win an argument and let the argument govern his facts. Because he needed the pagan past to look as bloody as the Christian present, he exaggerated ancient disasters and minimized recent ones; because he needed Rome's sack of 410 to seem mild, he described it as mild. The doctrine was right and the scholarship was bent to serve it, which is a lesson the church relearns in every generation of apologetics. A providence that must be propped up by a doctored chronicle is not being defended but insulted, for the God who “hath determined the times” (Act 17:26) does not need the times misreported.

The contrary corruption, and the dominant one now, is the historiography that rules providence out before it begins. Orosius at least asked the right question — who governs the rise and fall of kingdoms? — and answered it with Pro 21:1, that “the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD.” The modern account answers it with material cause alone and calls that neutrality. The recovery is to hold the doctrine firmly and the evidence honestly: God governs every empire, and the historian's task is to tell what actually happened, since the truth has no need of help.

pos: n. (Diognetus, the pagan inquirer to whom the anonymous second-century Epistle to Diognetus is addressed; by extension the epistle itself, the finest of the early apologies)
etymology: Greek Diognetos, from Dios, of Zeus, and gennetos, born — born of Zeus, a common name of rank.
biblical_def: Diognetus is a name we know nothing about, attached to a letter that has no author and survives in a single manuscript burnt in 1870. Yet the Epistle to Diognetus is the most beautiful thing the second century left us. It answers three questions a thoughtful pagan had asked — why Christians reject the gods, why they differ from the Jews, and why this people appeared so late — and it answers them in the register of the New Testament rather than of the schools. Its famous section describes believers as scattered through every city, obeying the laws, marrying and bearing children like other men, and yet citizens of another country: “They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world” (Joh 17:16), and “our conversation is in heaven” (Php 3:20). It is the doctrine of 1Pe 2:11 set out at length, the church as “strangers and pilgrims” who are the soul of the world they do not belong to. On the atonement it is unusually clear for its date: God gave His own Son as a ransom, the holy for the lawless, and there is no other way the unrighteous could be justified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pilgrim as a wanderer; a traveller; particularly one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
webster_full: PIL'GRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveller; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place, or to pay his devotion to the remains of dead saints.
2. In Scripture, one that has no settled habitation in this world, but considers himself a sojourner, whose home is heaven.
scriptures: They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
Php 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: The epistle's picture of Christians as the soul of the world is now quoted to recommend cultural accommodation, which is the reverse of what it says.
corruption_paragraphs: The letter is a favourite of writers urging the church to be winsome, embedded and inoffensive, and the quotation always stops halfway. The epistle does say believers conform to local custom in dress and diet and are good neighbours; it goes on to say that they are hated for no fault, slandered, put to death, and that they do not expose their children or share the common bed, which is precisely where they refused the custom of their city. The sentence about the soul in the body ends with the observation that the soul is shut up in a body which hates it. Accommodation in things indifferent and refusal in things commanded are the two halves of one argument, and only the first half gets cited.

The recovery is the whole doctrine of pilgrimage. “These all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13) describes a people whose citizenship is elsewhere and whose conduct here is therefore not negotiable with the neighbours. 1Pe 2:11 puts the two together in a breath: because they are strangers and pilgrims, they abstain. The epistle to Diognetus is not a manual for blending in; it is the earliest and clearest statement that a church fully present in its city and wholly unlike it is the only kind the world will either hate or believe.

“For our conversation is in heaven” (Php 3:20) — the citizenship it describes.
